title: Detection of Botnet
summary: This strategy detects the use of botnet infrastructure against your environment, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1584.005 (Compromise Infrastructure: Botnet). Rather than building their own servers, adversaries rent or build networks of compromised hosts and use them as proxies, spam relays, and command and control relays, which makes the source of traffic look like an ordinary consumer internet connection. Detection relies on network and identity telemetry: proxy and firewall logs, DNS request logs, authentication records from remote access services, and reputation feeds that map addresses to botnet families. The main failure mode is that a single connection from a residential address proves nothing, so the detection has to correlate repeated or scheduled contact from many hosts, unusual process-to-destination pairs, and known command and control port behaviour. A second failure mode is infrastructure churn: sinkhole and reputation feeds lag behind new botnet address rotation, so list-only matching produces short-lived coverage.

beginner.definition: A botnet is a large group of infected computers that an attacker controls remotely. This detection looks for signs that your users or servers are talking to that kind of network. It catches both infected machines and traffic that is being relayed through bots to hide the real source.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers use botnets so their real location stays hidden. Traffic relayed through a bot often comes from a home internet address, so it does not look like a known bad server. If a machine in your network is part of a botnet, it can send spam, spread malware, or attack other companies. That puts your name on abuse reports and can break your internet reputation.
howItWorks: Network devices and servers record connections, with the internal host, the outside address, the port, and the time.
The detection checks each destination address and name against reputation data linked to botnet activity.
It also looks for behaviour patterns, such as many hosts contacting one address on a fixed schedule.
Identity records show whether remote access logins come from consumer internet addresses used by bots.
Matches are grouped by internal host so one alert lists all the related connections.
The analyst checks the host, isolates it if needed, and confirms with an endpoint scan or memory check.
beginner.example: Imagine a shop where every delivery is signed for at the door. A single van from an unknown address is normal. But when fifty shops in the same chain all sign for parcels from one small flat on the same street, at the same minute each night, the security team starts asking questions. The flat is the botnet, and the shops are the hosts that keep calling it.
takeaways: Botnet traffic hides behind ordinary home internet addresses, so address lists alone are weak.
Group alerts by internal host, because one infected machine usually makes many connections.
Reputation feeds change daily, so refresh them and expect some missing coverage.

objectives: Describe how botnets are used as relays and command and control for later stages of an intrusion
Identify which network and identity log sources reveal botnet contact from inside your estate
Correlate address reputation with connection behaviour such as fixed intervals and many-to-one fan-in
Differentiate a compromised internal host from an external bot relaying traffic toward your services
Document a response path that covers containment, verification, and abuse notification
dataSources: Firewall or netflow logs of inbound and outbound sessions with source and destination address, port, and session duration
Web proxy logs showing repeated automated requests from internal hosts to the same external destination
DNS resolver logs with queried names, query intervals, and the client address making each request
VPN or remote access gateway authentication logs including source address, client name, and result
Threat intelligence feeds that map addresses and domains to known botnet families and sinkhole data
logic: The detection looks for structured, repetitive contact between one or more internal hosts and external endpoints that reputation data ties to botnet activity, or for behavioural signatures that are typical of botnet use such as a fixed beacon interval, a small consistent payload, or many hosts contacting one destination in the same short window. Fields that must be correlated are the internal host, the external destination, the port, the request interval, and the process or service account involved. The benign version of the same pattern is a scheduled software update, a monitoring agent, or a shared cloud service, which normally talks to documented vendor names, from a known process, across the whole estate at varied times. The malicious version usually comes from an unexpected process on a single host, keeps a tight interval, and matches a reputation hit.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Internal Host Beaconing to Known Botnet Infrastructure
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   category: firewall
# detection:
#   selection:
#     destination.ip|in: botnet_reputation_feed
#   selection_beacon:
#     event.action: connection
#     destination.port|in: [443, 8080, 4444, 6667]
#   filter_trusted:
#     process.name|endswith: updater.exe
#   condition: selection or selection_beacon and not filter_trusted
# level: high
falsePositives: Consumer grade remote workers connecting from home internet addresses that share address space with infected devices
Content delivery and peer to peer software that contacts many external peers on fixed intervals
Third party vulnerability scanners running from rented cloud or residential proxy ranges with customer approval
Threat intelligence and sinkhole research traffic generated by your own security team
Cheap internet of things devices on a guest network that phone home to a vendor service on a strict timer
tuningNotes: Begin with a filtered reputation feed that only contains confirmed command and control entries with a recent sighting, and refresh it at least daily, because stale entries create most of the noise. Add a filter for known sinkhole ranges, your own security scanning ranges, and approved peer to peer applications, then scope the behavioural half of the rule to server subnets and to hosts that have no business reason to beacon outbound. Baseline the normal outbound session interval per host group before you set a threshold, since a bad threshold on a busy server produces constant alerts. The coverage you give up is broad anomaly detection: a botnet using a mainstream content delivery network for relay will pass both halves of the rule, so keep a lower severity connection graph review for high value segments.
